claims.text: Adding 0.5–1 wt% graphene nanoplatelets to the HEA intermediate layer will increase its effective thermal conductivity.
Adding 0.5–1 wt% graphene nanoplatelets will preserve the HEA layer's structural integrity under plasma-facing conditions.
The initial HEA is single-phase and homogenized.
The initial HEA is produced by arc melting followed by thermal homogenization.
This HEA is currently used as an intermediate layer in plasma-facing reactor components.
Mechanical alloying followed by hot extrusion or forging can produce a uniform graphene dispersion with strong graphene–HEA interfacial bonding.
Graphene nanoplatelets at 0.5–1 wt% will form a spatially continuous network in the HEA.
The graphene network will provide enhanced heat-conduction pathways through the HEA.
Dispersed graphene nanoplatelets will reinforce the HEA microstructure and preserve its yield strength and overall structural integrity.
Graphene has inherently high thermal conductivity.
Uniformly dispersed graphene supplies additional electron and phonon conduction pathways that increase heat transfer through the HEA composite.
Graphene can maintain or slightly reinforce the HEA matrix without causing deleterious phase transformations or embrittlement.

At approximately 1000°C in helium under moderate-strain-rate mechanical loading, the graphene-enhanced HEA will retain higher thermal conductivity than the undoped control with little or no loss of yield strength or ductility.
Current undoped HEA intermediate layers have moderate heat-transfer properties.
Current undoped HEA intermediate layers have acceptable structural integrity.
Excess graphene addition or graphene aggregation could adversely affect the HEA microstructure.
Prolonged high-temperature plasma exposure and cyclic thermal-mechanical stress may destabilize the graphene dispersion or graphene–HEA interface.
